title: How to Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads — Go
summary:
Short answer: compare the tenant boundary before comparing upload latency. For a logistics receipt workflow, the browser should receive a short-lived upload URL for one server-selected object key, while the storage policy must prevent that URL from crossing tenants. S3, Cloudflare R2, and Wasabi can all be evaluated through that same contract because the important test is the trust boundary: who chooses the bucket, key, headers, and expiry, and what happens when a client retries?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. Those alerts changed how I look at direct uploads. A successful HTTP response is not proof that the receipt is attached to the right shipment. A retry can create a second object, and a copied upload URL can expose another tenant's prefix. The provider comparison belongs after those cases are defined.

title: Shadow AI Discovery and Data Loss Prevention Playbook
summary:
Shadow AI discovery is the part of AI governance that IT teams inherit without being asked. Nobody sends a memo announcing that the sales team pasted a customer contract into a chat tool, that an engineer connected a coding assistant to the production repository, or that finance trials four summarisation tools on last quarter's board pack. The usage simply exists, and the first question leadership asks is one nobody can answer from existing dashboards: how much of this is happening, and what data has left the building?

The comfortable answer, that the company has a policy and a list of approved tools, describes intent rather than reality. Discovery is a separate discipline with its own data sources, its own blind spots, and its own false positives. This playbook is the version I would run at a 100 to 1,000 person company with a small IT team and no enterprise SIEM: what signals to collect, what risks those signals reveal, and which controls are worth buying before the rest.<

title: Is It Safe to Delete ~/Library/Caches on a Mac? How to Clear Cache Safely
summary:
Yes—most subfolders inside ~/Library/Caches are safe to delete on a Mac, as long as you quit running apps first, remove only the contents inside (never the Caches folder itself), and skip Apple system caches and sensitive tool data. Apps automatically recreate their cache files the next time you open them, so the only normal side effect is a slightly slower first launch or re-downloading cached assets.

What you should not touch are macOS's system-wide /Library/Caches and /System/Library/Caches folders—macOS manages those itself. Also keep expectations realistic: clearing cache reclaims disk space, not RAM or CPU performance; in fact, rebuilding caches can briefly use a little extra disk and network activity right after cleanup.

title: How we keep a Laravel log ingest endpoint fast (Valkey buffer, batched ClickHouse writes)
summary:
We're building a hosted log tool on Laravel 13, and the part that took the most thought was ingestion. Clients send logs in bursts, sometimes thousands of lines a second, and the endpoint can't sit waiting on a database while that happens.

The request does almost nothing

It checks the token, pushes the batch into Valkey (Redis-compatible) and returns a 202. There are no MySQL queries in that path and no queue job per line.

Drainers do the writing

Separate long-running drainer processes, one per buffer shard, claim a batch of 500 to 1000 lines, insert it into ClickHouse, and only acknowledge it after the insert succeeded. Popping first and writing second looks simpler, but it loses lines if the process dies in between.
